text: Imagine holding half a billion dollars… in your hand.
Not in a bank. In a tiny steel USB drive.
There's just one problem. It's locked. And you've forgotten the password.
You get ten tries. You've already used eight.
Two left. Get them wrong… and the money is gone. Forever.
Go on. Try.
This isn't a thought experiment. It's happening right now, to a real person.
And when hackers offered to open it for him… he said no.
To understand why, we have to go back to 2011.
Stefan Thomas is a programmer. And in 2011, someone asked him to make a short animated video about a strange new thing called Bitcoin.
His payment? Seven thousand and two bitcoin.
Back then, that was basically pocket money.
So he stored the keys somewhere very safe: an IronKey.
An IronKey isn't a normal USB stick. It's built like a tiny bank vault. And it has one rule it never breaks.
Ten wrong passwords… and it destroys the key inside. No reset. No recovery. No 'forgot password' button.
So Stefan wrote his password on a piece of paper.
You can probably guess what happened to the paper.
He lost it.
For a while, it didn't matter. Bitcoin was cheap.
Then the price started to climb. A hundred dollars. A thousand. Ten thousand.
And every time it went up, that little drive got heavier.
So Stefan started guessing. The passwords he always used. Old favourites. Little variations.
Wrong. Wrong. Three… four… five… six… seven…
Eight.
Two left.
He told the New York Times: “I would just lay in bed and think about it. Then I would go to the computer with some new strategy, and it wouldn't work, and I would be desperate again.”
Think about that. A fortune within reach, every single night. And two chances to lose it forever.
In 2021, it was worth about two hundred and twenty million dollars. At bitcoin's peak, in October 2025, close to nine hundred million.
So… why not just break it open?
Because the IronKey remembers.
Every wrong guess is counted inside a sealed chip. Unplug it, leave it in a drawer for a year, plug it back in… still eight.
Try to drill into it, and you hit hard epoxy, built to stop exactly that.
Even Kingston, the company that makes IronKeys today, said it couldn't help. No backdoor. No master key.
So it's impossible. Right?
Stick around. And subscribe… I'm very good at waiting.
Here's the thing. Someone has already pulled off something like this.
Meet Joe Grand, a hardware hacker. In 2021, a man named Dan Reich came to him with about two million dollars in crypto, locked in a little wallet called a Trezor. He'd forgotten the PIN.
Twelve wrong guesses already. At sixteen, the wallet wipes itself. Four tries left.
So Joe didn't guess. He went after the chip.
During a firmware update, the wallet copies its PIN into memory. That memory is locked.
But Joe hit the chip with a tiny, perfectly timed glitch in its power… and for a split second, the lock blinked.
It took him twelve weeks of failures.
And then, the PIN appeared on his screen.
Two million dollars. Back.
So could the same trick work on Stefan's drive?
Not quite. That flaw was fixed back in 2017. And the IronKey is a much tougher machine.
But in 2023, a security company called Unciphered said it had found a way in.
Working with Wired, they took an IronKey of the same model, carved out its chip, dissolved the protective epoxy with acid…
…and ran about two hundred trillion password guesses.
It opened.
So they called Stefan with an offer: let us unlock your drive.
And Stefan… said no.
Why would anyone say no to half a billion dollars?
According to reports, he had already hired another team, and promised them a share if they succeeded.
So right now, somewhere, someone may be trying to open that drive.
And as of today, there's no public confirmation that anyone has.
And Stefan isn't alone.

In Wales, a man named James Howells says he threw away a hard drive with around eight thousand bitcoin on it, back in 2013. It's buried in a landfill. He spent years in court trying to dig it up. In 2025, he lost.
One estimate, from the blockchain firm Chainalysis, suggested that up to one in five bitcoins may be lost forever.
So how do you make sure this never happens to you?
Use a password manager, so your memory isn't the only backup.
Write your recovery codes down, and keep copies in two safe places. Not one piece of paper.
Test your backup before you need it.
And make sure someone you trust knows where to find it.
Stefan called it a painful memory, and said he hopes others can learn from his mistakes. He said he was depressed for a few weeks… then decided to look forward, and keep building.
So here's my question. Two guesses. More than half a billion dollars. Would you try them yourself… or hand the drive to a hacker? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because next time, we're digging into that landfill.
And I thought my sentence was bad.
Two guesses. I'll be waiting.
